anatomy.lede: The coelacanth carries features that vanished from almost every other living animal long ago: fleshy limb-like fins, a hinged skull and a lung that no longer breathes.

hotspots.label: Snout
hotspots.text: Inside the snout lies the rostral organ, whose structure suggests it detects weak electric fields.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: The large eye is tuned to the narrow band of blue light, around 480 nm, that reaches the coelacanth's depths.

hotspots.label: Lobed pectoral fin
hotspots.text: The paired fins grow from fleshy, muscular lobes and move in an alternating pattern, like the legs of a walking four-limbed animal.

hotspots.label: Pelvic fin
hotspots.text: The pelvic fins are lobed too, and join in the same alternating, limb-like movements as the pectoral fins.

hotspots.label: Second dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The coelacanth usually swims slowly by sculling with its second dorsal fin and its anal fin.

hotspots.label: Armoured scales
hotspots.text: Tiny, nearly invisible yearly growth rings on the scales revealed that coelacanths live for around a century.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: Although it usually moves slowly, a sudden flip of the tail fin lets the fish make a quick lunge.

stats.label: Share of the braincase filled by the brain

senses.lede: Coelacanths hunt at night in near-darkness. Their senses are tuned to a deep, dim, blue world.

senses.name: Blue-tuned vision
senses.text: The coelacanth appears to see with just two visual pigments, a rod pigment and a cone pigment, most sensitive at 478 nm and 485 nm. Both are shifted to match the blue light near 200 m depth.

senses.name: Rostral organ
senses.text: The structure of the rostral organ in the snout points to an electroreceptive role, and the fish may use it to scan the seabed for hidden prey.

senses.name: The headstand
senses.text: Coelacanths have been seen standing on their heads for two or three minutes. This may be a way of scanning the bottom with the rostral organ, or simply a reaction to submersible lights.

body.lede: Under its armoured skin the coelacanth is a museum of early vertebrate design, adapted to a cold, deep, slow life.

systems.title: A hinged skull
systems.text: It is the only living vertebrate whose braincase is split in two by an intracranial joint. A unique muscle flexes the front of the skull at this joint and boosts its bite force.

systems.title: A lung that stopped growing
systems.text: The earliest known embryo has a well-developed lung, but its growth stalls and in adults it is vestigial. A fatty organ develops alongside it and controls buoyancy instead.

systems.title: Slow metabolism
systems.text: Coelacanths extract oxygen poorly and have a slow metabolism, which fits their slow growth and very long lives.

genome.lede: Sequencing the coelacanth in 2013 settled an old question about which fish are our closest cousins, and showed a genome that has changed unusually little.

findings.title: Slowly evolving genes
findings.text: Its protein-coding genes have changed at roughly half the rate of tetrapod genes since the two lineages split, which may help explain why it looks so like its fossil relatives.

findings.title: A switch for building limbs
findings.text: A stretch of DNA near the HoxD genes, shared with tetrapods but not ray-finned fish, drove limb-specific activity when tested in mice, suggesting a fin enhancer was later reused for building hands and feet.

findings.title: Missing antibody
findings.text: Despite extensive searching, no genes for IgM, an antibody found in almost all other jawed vertebrates, were found; it has two IgW genes instead.

mind.lede: Coelacanths are hard to watch: most of what is known about their behaviour comes from submersible and camera observations at depth.

studies.title: Drift hunting
studies.text: Coelacanths are slow, night-time drift hunters, riding currents close to the seabed and taking cephalopods, eels, cuttlefish and deep-water fishes.

studies.title: Known by their spots
studies.text: The pattern of white blotches on each fish is unique, so researchers can recognise individuals from photographs and video.

studies.title: Shared caves
studies.text: Up to 13 or 14 coelacanths have been found resting together in one cave by day, although each forages alone at night.

survival.lede: Coelacanths have few natural enemies but almost no capacity to recover from losses.

tactics.title: Cave shelter
tactics.text: Daytime caves and ledges on steep rocky slopes give them shelter from predators.

tactics.title: Living cheaply
tactics.text: A slow metabolism lets them live on little food in deep, cool water of about 13–25 °C.

threats.title: Shark gillnets
threats.text: Off Tanzania, coelacanths are caught as bycatch in deep-set shark gillnets, which NOAA calls historically the most significant threat. The fishery has expanded over the last decade.

threats.title: Coastal development
threats.text: Deep-water port building brings pollution, sediment, underwater blasting and dredging into coelacanth habitat.

threats.title: Slow life, high risk
threats.text: With maturity at 40 to 69 years and a five-year pregnancy, coelacanths may be more threatened than once thought.

life.lede: The coelacanth has one of the slowest life histories of any fish: decades to grow up, years to give birth.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Eggs are huge, about 9 cm across and over 325 g, and are fertilised and kept inside the mother.

stages.name: Embryo
stages.text: The young develop inside the mother for around five years, according to scale-based estimates, possibly the longest pregnancy of any animal with a backbone.

stages.name: Newborn
stages.text: Pups are born live at an estimated 35–38 cm long. One 179 cm female caught off Mozambique in 1991 carried 26 near-term pups.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Scale growth rings suggest sexual maturity comes very late, somewhere between 40 and 69 years of age.
